4.4 Exercises 4- Exercises on normal subgroups, simplicity and Lagrange’s Theorem (S) Question 4.4.1. Let G be a group with H ≤ G and N ⊴ G. Prove that H ∩ N is a normal subgroup of H. Question 4.4.2. Prove that S5 has no subgroup of order 9. Question 4.4.3. Let G be a group with H ≤ G and N ⊴ G. Prove that HN = {hk ∶ h ∈ H, k ∈ N } is equal to N H = {kh ∶ k ∈ N, h ∈ H}. Question 4.4.4. Let p be a prime and let G be a group with ∣G∣ = p. (a) Prove that the only subgroups of G are ⟨eG⟩ and G (b) Hence prove that G is cyclic. Question 4.4.5. Let G be a group with H ≤ G and N ⊴ G. Prove that HN ≤ G. Question 4.4.6. Show that C3 ⊴ S3. Question 4.4.7. Recall that FS(Z) denotes the finitary permutations of Z, and consists of permutations of Z that move only finitely many elements of Z. (a) Does the permutation (1 3 5)(6 8 10) lie in FS(Z)? (b) Let τ be the permutation which maps each n ∈ Z to −n. Does τ lie in FS(Z)? (c) Prove that FS(Z) ≤ Sym(Z). (d) Is FS(Z) abelian? (e) Prove that FS(Z) ⊴ Sym(Z). Note: for a general set X, the group FS(X) is called the finitary symmetric group on X, and is always a normal subgroup of Sym(X).

Hint. (Question 4.4.1) Show that for all h ∈ H and all k ∈ H ∩ N we have that h−1kh ∈ H ∩ N . Hint. (Question 4.4.2) Use Lagrange’s Theorem. Hint. (Question 4.4.3) Use the Order Switching Lemma to show HN ⊆ N H and vice versa. Do not assume the group is abelian! Hint. (Question 4.4.4) To prove (a) use Lagrange’s Theorem. To prove (b) use (a) to consider what any cyclic subgroup ⟨g⟩ ≤ G must look like. Hint. (Question 4.4.5) Use the Order Switching Lemma to check the conditions of the Quick Subgroup Test. Do not assume the group is abelian! Hint. (Question 4.4.6) Write out all the elements of S3 and C3, then ask yourself: What is the product of a 2-cycle with a 3-cycle? What is the product of two 2-cycles? What is the product of two 3-cycles? Use this to show normality.
